pages.text: Scotland and Netherlands share series after third ODI rained off - BBC Sport Image source, Cricket Scotland Image caption, There was no play under the shadow of the Wallace Monument Published 1 September 2026 Scotland and the Netherlands have tied their one-day-international series 1-1 after the third match was abandoned without a ball being bowled at Stirling County following heavy and persistent rain throughout the day. The series was arranged at short notice as the Dutch women sought to regain their ODI ranking and avoid a substantial funding cut next year. The visitors won the opening match by 58 runs at Clydesdale, with the Scots securing a convincing nine-wicket victory in a rain-affected second in Stirling. However, it does mean that the Dutch have done enough to secure their ranking and much-needed funds. pages.text: Scotland beat Canada by nine runs to reach World Cup Qualifier - BBC Sport Image source, Ian Jacobs Image caption, Fin McCreath was Scotland's top scorer with 112 Published 7 August 2026 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 tri-series, Forthill Scotland 281-7 (50 overs): McCreath 112; Shirzad 3-55 Canada 272 (49.2): Samra 78; McMullen 3-43 Scotland won by nine runs Scorecard Scotland held on for a nervy nine-run victory over Canada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 match in Forfarshire. Fin McCreath's 112, his first international century, helped the hosts post 281-7 at Forthill. Canada hit 50 inside eight overs thanks to Yuvraj Sumra (78), but they fell to 181-7 only for a partnership of 84 by Ansh Patel and captain Saad Bin Zafar to take them close to their target before George Munsey's catch secured Scotland's win with four balls remaining. Scotland are now assured a place at next year's Qualifier as Canada cannot catch them in the League 2 standings. It was the first game of the tri-series, which also involves the United Arab Emirates, to beat the wet weather after two washouts. Grange batter McCreath reached his century from 135 balls in the 47th over. pages.description: Scotland level their one-day international series with the Netherlands at 1-1 after a thumping nine-wicket victory in a rain-affected match in Stirling.
pages.text: Scotland beat Netherlands by nine wickets to level ODI series - BBC Sport Image source, Cricket Scotland Image caption, Scotland made short work of chasing down the Dutch total after a wet morning in Stirling Published 31 August 2026 Second one-day international, Stirling Netherlands 129-9 (32 overs): De Leede 58; Maqsood 3-20, Carter 2-18 Scotland 130-1 (16.2 overs): S Bryce 70*, Carter 33* Scotland won by nine wickets Scorecard Scotland levelled their one-day international series with the Netherlands at 1-1 after a thumping nine-wicket victory in a rain-affected match in Stirling. Sarah Bryce, captaining the side in the absence of her sister Kathyrn, led the way with an unbeaten 70 as the hosts chased down their target of 130 in just over half of their allotted 32 overs, in a game which was originally scheduled for Sunday but fell foul of the weather. The Dutch had enjoyed a 58-run win in Glasgow on Friday and this was another one-sided contest. Darcy Carter made an early breakthrough, taking the wickets of Netherlands openers Phebe Molkenboer and Sanya Khurana, who had piled on more than 150 in last week's encounter. Abtaha Maqsood also took two quick wickets to leave the visitors reeling on 39-4. Maqsood struck again but Babette de Leede made 58 before being run out, while Caroline de Lange added 20 on the way to their total of 129-9. Scotland lost Maryam Faisal after four balls but Carter (33 not out) and Bryce made sure of a comprehensive success. pages.description: Scotland's bowlers make short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progress to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai.
pages.text: Scotland coast to win over Ireland as both reach Super Six phase - BBC Sport Image source, ICC/Getty Images Image caption, Kirstie Gordon took four wickets for just four runs in Dubai Published 18 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy Ireland 71 (19.3 overs): Lewis 20; Gordon 4-4, Maqsood 3-15 Scotland 72-2 (8.3 overs): Carter 30, Fraser 21 Scotland win by eight wickets Scotland's bowlers made short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progressed to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai. Kirstie Gordon ripped through the Irish top order, the left-arm spinner taking four wickets for just four runs. Abtaha Maqsood claimed three wickets, Kathryn Bryce struck twice and Priyanaz Chatterji picked up her 50th T20 International wicket as Ireland were dismissed for just 71. Captain Gaby Lewis top scored for Ireland on 20, with Georgina Dempsey (12), Abbi Harrison (11) and Jane Maguire (11*) the others to reach double figures. In reply, Darcey Carter (30) and Katherine Fraser (21) enjoyed a 53-run opening partnership, with Kathryn Bryce (7*) and Sarah Bryce (4*) steering Scotland home in the ninth over. Scotland finished second behind unbeaten Sri Lanka in Group A, with Ireland in third place. Netherlands and Pakistan are guaranteed passage from Group B as Zimbabwe and Bangladesh vie for the remaining spot. pages.text: Scotland men's internationals to be shown live on BBC - BBC Sport Image source, SNS Image caption, Live coverage of Steve Clarke's Scotland starts with a visit to Greece Published 7 March 2025 The BBC has agreed an exclusive contract to broadcast live all Scotland men's international football matches in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup. It is part of a wider deal agreed with European governing body Uefa that also includes matches involving Northern Ireland and Wales - the first time the broadcaster has secured live rights for all three of the UK's devolved nations. The contract includes all 14 live Scotland matches, beginning with the first leg of the Nations League play-off in Greece on 20 March and including June friendlies against Iceland and Leichtenstein as well as World Cup qualifiers. Director BBC Scotland Hayley Valentine said: "I'm so excited that millions of Scotland fans will now be able to enjoy free-to-air access to all Scotland's international matches. pages.description: Glasgow's Titwood has been chosen as the proposed Scottish venue for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2030.
pages.text: Scotland propose Titwood venue for 2030 T20 World Cup - BBC Sport Image source, SNS Image caption, Titwood has been the home of Clydesdale Cricket Club since 1876 Published 11 November 2026 Glasgow's Titwood has been chosen as the proposed Scottish venue for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2030. Home of Clydesdale Cricket Club since 1876, the ground is in the Pollokshields area of the city. The board of Cricket Scotland say their decision came following "engagement and consultation with the ICC, ECB and other strategic partners". The 2030 World Cup is being co-hosted by England & Wales, Scotland and Ireland. It will be the first major tournament in Scotland since the 1999 Cricket World Cup when The Grange in Edinburgh staged two group matches. Titwood would require a major overhaul and the next steps include talks with the Scottish and UK governments. Scotland's women met the Netherlands in a one-day international at Titwood in August, while the men played six T20 internationals there in June 2025. pages.title: Scotland women beaten by Sri Lanka in second Emerging Trophy group fixture - BBC Sport
pages.description: Scotland women succumb to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy Group A fixture.
pages.text: Scotland women beaten by Sri Lanka in second Emerging Trophy group fixture - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Published 13 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy Scotland 111-8 (20 overs): Carter 62; Masqood 3-18 Sri Lanka 115-6 (18.1 overs): Gunaratne 49; Kumari 2-15, Sandeepani 2-18 Sri Lanka win by four wickets Scotland succumbed to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy campaign Group A fixture. Having opened with victory over Papua New Guinea, the Scots batted first against Sri Lanka but were restricted to 111-8 in Ajman, United Arab Emirates. Darcey Carter top scored on 62 runs off 55 deliveries while Sathya Sandeepani and Sugandika Kumari took two wickets each. Sri Lanka's Vishmi Gunaratne amassed 49 runs off 41 deliveries, with captain Harshitha Samarawickrama contributing 24. Abatha Masqood took three wickets, becoming the Scots' top wicket taker in WT20Is, her 77 surpassing current captain Kathryn Bryce. Ten nations are participating in the UAE, split into two groups of five before a Super Six stage to determine the final on 25 November. Scotland play the hosts next, with UAE having opened with defeat by Ireland, who picked up a first win. In this role, he oversees a multi-billion-dollar portfolio dedicated to advancing the commercial deployment and scaling of innovative energy, materials, and industrial manufacturing technologies. His leadership supports CMEI’s mission to secure stable domestic supply chains, strengthen American manufacturing, and steward federal resources to provide affordable, reliable, and secure energy for the nation. Mr. Pappano has dedicated nearly 35 years of service to the United States Navy as a submarine officer and acquisition leader, including at the rank of Vice Admiral before retiring in May 2025. Throughout his career, Mr. Pappano not only commanded at sea, but shaped the future of undersea warfare and strategic deterrence for generations to come. Pappano served onboard five submarines, including command of USS Buffalo (SSN 715) while forward deployed in Guam. Assignments ashore included submarine tactics development, Navy nuclear power training, defense international security policy, and Navy programming. After selection as an acquisition professional, Pappano served as Major Program Manager for the Strategic and Attack Submarine Program Office (PMS 392). pages.description: The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout in the UK have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle.
pages.text: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Games currently cannot be shown live between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 29 October 2026 The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle. The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season. BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon. The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes. Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time. While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday. Other leagues now tend to stagger kick-off times so the top divisions do not all play at the same time, meaning the blackout could not be applied. In the UK, 3pm remains the traditional, default kick-off time for all leagues from the very top down through non-league. SCIENCE LAELAPS Scrappy Fossils Yield Possible Dinosaur Blood Cells By Riley Black Published June 16, 2015 • 8 min read Last week, a little movie called Jurassic World debuted. You might have heard something about it . Paleontologists certainly have been jawing about it for a while, particularly how the movie’s dinosaurs stack up against the actual animals emerging from the rock.* But all the arguments about enfluffled dinosaurs and bunny hands have missed a more fundamental issue – could scientists ever recover enough intact dinosaur goo to populate a real Jurassic World? When the first Jurassic Park premiered in 1993, finding non-avian dinosaur DNA seemed a certainty. Two days before the official release of the movie Raúl Cano and colleagues announced that they had sequenced the DNA of a 135-120 million year old, amber-encased weevil. Woodward and colleagues announced that they had sequenced DNA from an 80 million year old dinosaur bone fragment. It seemed that life had found a way. Screening for Type 1 Diabetes Apr. 17, 2026 Key points Type 1 diabetes develops in stages and may start a long time before a person needs insulin. People at high risk for type 1 diabetes can benefit from screening before symptoms appear. Knowing they’re in the early stages of type 1 diabetes can help people notice symptoms and avoid serious complications. Who should be offered screening? People with a family member who has type 1 diabetes are 15 times more likely to develop type 1 than the general population and should be offered screening. It’s important to note, though, that most people who develop type 1 don’t have a family member with the condition. Screening can begin at 2 years old. Why get screened? Type 1 diabetes is often an emergency diagnosis. A person likely doesn't know they have type 1 diabetes until a serious complication happens, such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is a medical emergency and can be life-threatening if untreated. In the United States, 30% to 40% of children have DKA when they are first diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. pages.text: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic By Craig Welch Photographs by Thomas Peschak 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. To see all that’s hopeful and appalling about the way we treat sea turtles , there’s no better place to start than the Burj Al Arab Jumeirah hotel. This shimmering tower of blue and white glass is shaped like the jib of a sailboat bound for shore. It rose two decades ago on an artificial island amid the steel forest of construction cranes that is Dubai, part of the United Arab Emirates. A royal suite, at 8,396 square feet, comes with a private cinema and 17 pillow options. A weekend stay can top $50,000. I have come here, though, to see its nonpaying guests. ( Saving Sea Turtles) Passing a fleet of white Rolls-Royces, I meet British expat marine biologist David Robinson. We take an elevator down to a parking garage and walk by Lamborghinis to our destination: a labyrinth of pipes and plastic pools, the intensive care unit of an elaborate marine turtle hospital. In one tub a green sea turtle struggles with internal organ damage. One floor up, sick, critically endangered hawksbills fill aquariums. Blood seeps from a dying leatherback harpooned by an indigenous hunter near Indonesia’s Kei Islands. Leatherbacks are the largest of the seven sea turtle species and one of the most imperiled. The West Pacific population has fewer than a thousand females. A flatback sea turtle kicks up sand while digging a nest on Crab Island, off Australia’s northeast coast. NPS The first blooms of spring. The first frost. The first dusting of snow. The signs and timing of the seasons is a finely tuned natural process. The interplay of temperature and daylight activates these changes and the subsequent plant and animal responses. A slight shift in any of these may mean that vegetation will no longer grow in a certain location or appear at a different time of year. Without plants, animals who eat them may struggle to survive or may have to move elsewhere to find better food. The consequences may extend to the entire ecosystem, including humans. In both Skagway and Nome, everyone agreed that spring is arriving earlier and fall is starting later. This not only makes for a longer growing season for gardeners, but it affects the arrival and departure timing of migratory animals that people hunt and may shift the location of where the animals are found. Alyssa Schukar "The museum of the past must be set aside, reconstructed, transformed...into a nursery of living thoughts,” George Brown Goode, the first curator of the Smithsonian’s Arts and Industries Building (AIB), wrote in 1889. “It should be a house full of ideas.” AIB opened in 1881 as the first United States National Museum with a radical new philosophy. Museums could do more than research and showcase; they could teach and inspire as well. Thousands flocked to the Mall’s newest building to see firsthand the inventions that were changing the world: the electric light bulb, the steam locomotive, Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone. AIB pioneered many of the Smithsonian features we now consider essential: descriptive labels to explain what people saw, new ways of organizing displays to tell stories, and even “living animal” collections (an initiative that would eventually grow into the National Zoo). By the time I worked as a curator at the National Museum of American History , AIB was serving even younger audiences: My daughter attended preschool in the building that had once housed the Star-Spangled Banner and the Spirit of St. Louis . pages.text: See how we’re reimagining dinosaurs in today’s ‘golden age’ of paleontology | National Geographic This story appears in the October 2020 issue of National Geographic magazine. On a chilly January afternoon, Susannah Maidment stands on the shore of a London lake, staring down a pack of dinosaurs. Maidment, a curator at the U.K.’s Natural History Museum, has come with me to tour Crystal Palace Park, which in 1854 included the world’s first public dinosaur showcase. The sculptures were a smash hit at their unveiling and sparked the dinomania that’s been with us ever since. More than a century before Steven Spielberg dazzled the world with Jurassic Park , the Crystal Palace dinosaurs drew two million visitors a year for three decades straight, and Charles Dickens name-dropped one in his novel Bleak House . ( Paleontologists Reveal the Identity of ‘Predator X’) To grant us a detailed look at these 166-year-old monuments, Ellinor Michel and Sarah Jayne Slaughter, trustees with the nonprofit Friends of Crystal Palace Dinosaurs, guide us through a metal gate to the banks of the lake, where we don waders to make our crossing. I misjudge my first step and fall into the water, clambering onto the island’s shore, dripping wet and smelling of pond scum. “Welcome to Dinosaur Island!” Slaughter exclaims, grinning from ear to ear. Some 166 million years ago in what is now Oxfordshire County, England, the ground trembled with the footfalls of the first dinosaur to be scientifically described, Megalosaurus.
